newsitem.title: FRANCE: Airbus says Boeing-MD merger won't alter rivalry.
newsitem.headline: Airbus says Boeing-MD merger won't alter rivalry.

text.p: A merger plan between U.S. rival aerospace firms Boeing and McDonnell Douglas (MD) will not alter the competitive threat to Europe's Airbus Industrie, an Airbus spokesman said on Sunday.

McDonnell Douglas "hasn't been a competitor in the civilian aircraft business for a number of years," the spokesman said. "So it hasn't altered the equation in the commercial field at all for Airbus."
The merger, which will create the world's biggest aerospace firm with 1997 turnover of about $48 billion, had been expected since McDonnell Douglas dropped plans for a new plane, he said.

"It was expected that Douglas would have to look in the civil field for its fortunes elsewhere, or merge, or opt out of the business all together," the spokesman said. Boeing was the obvious merger candidate, he added.
MD decided in October to drop plans to build the MD-XX wide body passenger jet, which would have doomed it to niche player status with its two current products, the MD-11 and MD-80/90.
In the military sector, it lost a key competition in November to build the Joint Strike Fighter (JSF), potentially worth $200 billion. It has not won a new fighter contest since its F15 win in 1969.

Boeing can already use its size to bear down on suppliers to cut costs and raise capital on the financial markets, the Airbus spokesman said, adding that Boeing also enjoys political support from the White House for sales campaigns.
Earlier this month, after an announcement that Boeing and McDonnell Douglas were cooperating on future wide-bodies, Airbus said "It doesn't change our agenda."

Airbus has said it wants to win at least half the world passenger plane market by the end of the decade. Historically it has held around 30 percent, Boeing 60 percent and McDonnell Douglas 10 percent.
